newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN TRUTH BODY TO PERUSE APARTHEID-ERA FILES.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN TRUTH BODY TO PERUSE APARTHEID-ERA FILES.

text.p: South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission would soon examine secret state documents in the hope they could cast light on the shadowy dealings of past intelligence agencies, an official said on Tuesday.

"Those documents are available and we are in the process of getting access to them," truth commission research director Charles Villa-Vicencio told a news conference, adding that State Security Council (SSC) documents would also be studied.
"There are either tape recordings or transcripts of the State Security Council meetings," Villa-Vicencio elaborated.
Convicted former police hit-squad leader Eugene de Kock testified during his murder trial this week that the SSC knew and sanctioned actions against anti-apartheid activists.
The SSC was a body whose members included former president P.W. Botha and leading cabinet members during the apartheid years. Nothing has been proved against them, however.

South Africa's African National Congress-led government suggested recently that in the build-up to the 1994 all-race general elections sensitive documents were disposed of by bureaucrats eager to cover their past deeds.
"These reports are indeed a matter of concern to us, but we are at an early stage," Villa-Vicencio said.
"Primarily what we want is to go and have a look at specific documents so as answer specific questions...and we've had a lot cooperation for that," he added.

Villa-Vicencio's department must help compile the TRC's report on 30 years of South Africa's race conflict. The report will be submitted to President Nelson Mandela at the end of next year, when the commission is scheduled to complete its work.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission was set up last year to probe human rights violations during the country's turbulent past. It is chaired by retired Anglican Archbishop Desmond Tutu and has the power to grant amnesty to violators who come clean.

"We can't finish in two years but we've got to finish in two years and within that limited period of time you can only produce what you can produce," Villa-Vicencio said, sharing the concern over the timeframe also voiced by Tutu.

Commission spokesman John Allen meanwhile announced on Tuesday that senior officers from the apartheid-era South African Defence Force (SADF) would make a written submission before the truth body on September 30.
The submission would be about the force's activities from 1960 to 1993. Allen was unable to name the officers who would represent the SADF.
